question_text: Define the law of Segregation and the law of Independent Assortment.

mark_split.label: Why it is called purity of gametes

insider_note: Both laws are about GAMETES. Say the word gamete in both definitions and neither can be confused for the other.

page_header: Principles of Inheritance and Variation (Botany-II) · 4 marks

steps.label: Law of segregation
steps.margin_note: Do not blend, do segregate, one per gamete. All three parts.
lines: The LAW OF SEGREGATION states that the two
alleles of a gene, when present together in a
heterozygote, do NOT fuse or blend.
They remain distinct, and SEGREGATE from each
other during MEIOSIS.
Each gamete therefore carries only ONE of the
two alleles.
steps.why: If alleles blended, the recessive character could never reappear unchanged in F2 — so the law is what the F2 observation forces.
common_mistakes: Saying the alleles blend. The whole law is that they do NOT.
Leaving out meiosis. Segregation happens during MEIOSIS, when gametes form.
steps.memory_tip: They travel together but they never mix.

steps.label: Why it is called purity of gametes
steps.margin_note: The alternative name and why it fits. This is a whole mark.
lines: The law is also called the LAW OF PURITY OF
GAMETES.
A gamete is PURE because it carries only one
allele of a pair, never both and never a
mixture.
This law has NO exceptions.
steps.why: A gamete is haploid, so it can only carry one of the two alleles — the law follows directly from meiosis rather than being an extra assumption.
common_mistakes: Saying gametes carry both alleles. A gamete carries ONE.
Leaving out the alternative name. It is what the question is often asked by.
steps.memory_tip: One allele per gamete, so the gamete is pure.

steps.label: Law of independent assortment
steps.margin_note: Definition plus the four gamete types. The gamete list proves the law.
lines: The LAW OF INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT
states that when two individuals differ in TWO OR
MORE pairs of contrasting characters, the
inheritance of one pair of factors is
INDEPENDENT of the other pair.
So a dihybrid YyRr makes FOUR kinds of gamete —
YR, Yr, yR, yr — in equal numbers.
steps.why: Two gene pairs on different chromosomes line up independently at meiosis, so every combination of them is equally likely in the gametes.
common_mistakes: Saying the two characters are inherited together. They are inherited INDEPENDENTLY.
Giving two kinds of gamete for a dihybrid. A double heterozygote makes FOUR.
steps.memory_tip: Two coins tossed together: each lands on its own.

steps.label: Which cross each comes from
steps.margin_note: Both sources, the 9:3:3:1 ratio, and the limitation. The limitation is worth the line.
lines: The law of SEGREGATION is based on the results
of the MONOHYBRID cross.
The law of INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT is
based on the results of the DIHYBRID cross, which gives
the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio in F₂.
Independent assortment holds only for genes on
DIFFERENT chromosomes.
steps.why: Genes on the same chromosome tend to travel together, so the law has a real limit — which is exactly what linkage is.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two crosses. Segregation comes from the MONOHYBRID cross.
Saying independent assortment always holds. It fails for LINKED genes on the same chromosome.
steps.memory_tip: One character gives segregation; two give assortment.

elements.text: Four kinds of gamete, in equal numbers

steps.why: Both laws are statements about gametes, so drawing the gametes a heterozygote and a dihybrid actually make is the shortest way to show both at once.
common_mistakes: Drawing a gamete carrying Tt. A gamete carries ONE allele: T or t.
Drawing two kinds of gamete from YyRr. A dihybrid makes FOUR.
Drawing the four dihybrid gametes in unequal numbers. They are formed in EQUAL numbers.
steps.memory_tip: Two from one gene pair, four from two gene pairs.
